Red codling (Pseudophycis bachus) commonly reaches a maximum total length of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] in Australian waters, a size that places it among the larger members of the Moridae family. Field surveys conducted across the continental shelf indicate that individuals attaining this ultimate length are typically older specimens exceeding a decade in age. The growth trajectory of this species is characterised by a rapid initial phase during the first few years, followed by a pronounced deceleration as fish approach their asymptotic size. This pattern is consistent with the life history strategy observed in many demersal gadiforms inhabiting temperate ecosystems. Length-frequency distributions derived from trawl catches show that the majority of the population clusters between 40 and 70 centimeters, with only a modest proportion of individuals reaching the upper limit of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters]. Such size truncation may reflect the combined effects of fishing pressure and natural mortality on larger cohorts. The species displays moderate sexual dimorphism in ultimate size, with females tending to achieve slightly greater lengths than males, although the maximum recorded value remains consistent across sexes and geographic regions.

Sexual maturation in female Red codling from Australian populations is attained at a total length of 31.5 centimeters [Lp = 31.5 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the first detectable signs of gonadal recrudescence. This length at puberty has been validated through histological examination of ovarian tissue in specimens collected during routine biomass surveys. In contrast, males reach sexual maturity at a noticeably smaller total length of 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters], a difference that reflects the typical pattern of protandrous or earlier male maturation observed in many teleost fishes. The divergence in size at puberty between the sexes likely stems from differential energetic allocation strategies, where females require a larger body size to accommodate the metabolic demands of egg production. Field data from the Great Australian Bight confirm that this size threshold is relatively stable across years, suggesting a robust physiological constraint. Both sexes continue to grow after reaching maturity, although the annual increment diminishes markedly following the onset of reproductive activity.

The wet weight of newly hatched Red codling larvae is extremely low at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value derived directly from the egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters and the assumption of spherical geometry. This minute birth mass places the species firmly among the category of small-egged marine teleosts that produce numerous, pelagic offspring. Yolk-sac larvae depend entirely on endogenous reserves during the initial days post-hatching, with the attendant risk of starvation if exogenous feeding onset is delayed beyond the point of no return. The small size of the newly emerged larvae also renders them highly vulnerable to a broad spectrum of planktonic predators during the early larval phase. Despite this fragility, the high fecundity of adult females compensates for the elevated mortality rates experienced during the pelagic egg and larval stages. Comparisons with related morid species indicate that a wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] is consistent with the conservative reproductive strategy typical of the family.

Females reaching the size threshold of 31.5 centimeters in total length achieve a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 482 grams [Wwp = 482 grams], reflecting the allometric relationship between length and mass in this species. Males, by contrast, attain puberty at a considerably lower wet weight of 193 grams [Wwp = 193 grams], a value that aligns with their smaller length at first maturation. This pronounced difference in body mass at sexual maturity highlights the contrasting reproductive energetics between the sexes; females must accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the production of large numbers of pelagic eggs. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adult Red codling has been estimated at 16,300 grams [Wwi = 16,300 grams], representing the maximum body mass achievable under optimal conditions. This value is derived from the asymptotic length and the empirically determined length-weight conversion, and it positions the species as one of the heavier members of the Australian morid assemblage. The substantial gap between the wet weight at puberty for females (482 grams [Wwp = 482 grams]) and the ultimate wet weight of 16,300 grams [Wwi = 16,300 grams] indicates a prolonged period of somatic growth following the onset of reproduction.

Under stable thermal conditions of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] typical of the continental shelf habitat, the maximum batch fecundity of Red codling has been estimated at approximately 82,192 eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 82,192 eggs per batch], with a spawning frequency of approximately 365 batches per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 batches per year]. This exceptionally high reproductive output is characteristic of batch-spawning marine teleosts that release multiple clutches over an extended breeding season. The sustained water temperature is thought to optimise both vitellogenic rates and the duration of the spawning period, allowing females to maximise lifetime fecundity. Correspondingly, the maximum recorded lifespan for Red codling under these same thermal conditions is 2,190 days [am = 2,190 days], equivalent to approximately six years at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Tag-recapture studies have confirmed that few individuals exceed this longevity, suggesting that natural senescence imposes a firm upper boundary on the species' life history. The combination of high batch fecundity and a lifespan of 2,190 days [am = 2,190 days] underscores a life history strategy heavily skewed toward early and prolific reproduction at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C].
